stories.title: Dylan Plugs In at Newport
stories.dek: The July night that split a folk festival
stories.body:
By the summer of 1965 Bob Dylan was the most closely watched songwriter in America. Only a few years earlier he had been a young singer in the coffeehouses of Greenwich Village, playing an acoustic guitar and singing songs about injustice. The folk community had embraced him as its leader. The Newport Folk Festival, in Rhode Island, was the center of that world, and Dylan had played there two years in a row to rapturous crowds.

But his music was changing. In March he had released Bringing It All Back Home, with an electric side, and in June he had gone into a New York studio and recorded a long, snarling song called "Like a Rolling Stone". An organist named Al Kooper, who had only come to watch, sat down at the keyboard and improvised a part that gave the track its distinctive sound. When the record came out in July, it climbed the charts.

Dylan arrived at Newport on July 25 with a band that included members of the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, including guitarist Mike Bloomfield. They had rehearsed a loud, rough set the night before. Many in the audience, expecting a solo acoustic performance, did not know what was coming.

The band walked on stage in the evening and played three songs: "Maggie's Farm", "Like a Rolling Stone" and "It Takes a Lot to Laugh, It Takes a Train to Cry". The sound was loud and, by most accounts, poorly mixed. There were boos. Whether they were aimed at the electric guitars, at the muddy sound, or at the short set is still a matter of debate among those who were there. Dylan left the stage, and later came back with an acoustic guitar to sing "It's All Over Now, Baby Blue" and "Mr. Tambourine Man", a gesture some saw as a farewell to the folk world.

Over the years the story has been embroidered. A popular legend has Pete Seeger threatening to cut the sound cables with an axe, though Seeger himself said he was upset only because he could not understand the words. The truth is that Dylan did not abandon folk music so much as stretch it, bringing the poetry of the coffeehouse into the volume of rock and roll.

A year later, on a tour of England, an audience member in Manchester shouted "Judas!" at him. Dylan told his band to play it loud. He had made his choice. Within a few years many folk singers were plugging in, and the line between folk and rock had blurred for good.

stories.title: Tapestry
stories.dek: A Brill Building songwriter finds her own voice
stories.body:
In the early 1960s Carole King was a teenage songwriter working in an office building on Broadway in New York, alongside other young songwriters who turned out hit after hit. With her husband, the lyricist Gerry Goffin, she wrote "Will You Love Me Tomorrow", which became a No. 1 hit for the Shirelles when she was only 18. She also wrote songs such as "Up on the Roof" for the Drifters and "(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman" for Aretha Franklin. Millions knew her songs, but almost nobody knew her name.

By the end of the decade her marriage with Goffin had ended. King moved to Laurel Canyon, a hillside neighborhood in Los Angeles where musicians such as Joni Mitchell and James Taylor lived. It was an informal, friendly scene, and she began to perform her own songs, often accompanying herself on piano. Producer Lou Adler encouraged her to make a record.

She recorded Tapestry in early 1971 at A&M Studios, working with a small group of friends, including Taylor on guitar and backing vocals. The songs were direct, honest and sung in a warm, unfussy voice. "It's Too Late" was a calm farewell to a love that had faded. "So Far Away" described the pain of distance. Even songs she had written for others, like "A Natural Woman" and "Will You Love Me Tomorrow", took on new meaning when she sang them herself. "You've Got a Friend" was a simple promise of loyalty, and Taylor recorded his own version.

The album came out in February 1971, and it was a huge success. It spent 15 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard album chart and stayed on the chart for more than 300 weeks. At the 1972 Grammy Awards, King won four trophies: Album of the Year, Record of the Year for "It's Too Late", Song of the Year for "You've Got a Friend" and Best Pop Vocal Performance, Female. It became one of the best-selling albums of all time.

The record also helped define a new style. The singer-songwriter era was built on personal, reflective songs, and Tapestry became its most visible monument. King had spent a decade writing hits in the shadows. In one winter, she became a star in her own right, and she showed that a woman at a piano with her own words could fill a stadium.

stories.title: The Sound of Silence, Remixed
stories.dek: The flop that turned into a No. 1 hit
stories.body:
Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel had known each other since they were boys in Forest Hills, Queens. As teenagers they had recorded a minor hit under the name Tom and Jerry, and in the early 1960s they began playing as a folk duo in Greenwich Village. In 1964 they signed with Columbia Records and made an acoustic album, Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M. It included a quiet, haunting song Simon had written called "The Sound of Silence".

The album sold very poorly. The two friends drifted apart. Garfunkel went back to his graduate studies at Columbia University, and Simon moved to England, where he played in folk clubs and recorded a solo album. It looked as though the duo was finished.

Back in New York, the folk-rock boom was starting. The Byrds had topped the charts with an electric version of Dylan's "Mr. Tambourine Man". Tom Wilson, a Columbia producer who had been working with Bob Dylan, noticed that radio stations in Boston and Florida were playing "The Sound of Silence" from the old album. In June 1965 he went into a studio with the same musicians who had played on Dylan's "Like a Rolling Stone" sessions, and he added electric guitar, bass and drums to Simon and Garfunkel's original recording. He did not tell the duo, and he did not ask.

Columbia released the remixed version as a single in September 1965. Simon and Garfunkel had not been consulted, and they were reportedly surprised by the result. But it caught on in a hurry. On the chart dated January 1, 1966, it reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.

Simon returned to America, and the two reunited to record a new album, Sounds of Silence, which came out in January 1966. They went on to a run of hits, including "Mrs. Robinson", "Scarborough Fair" and "Bridge Over Troubled Water", before parting in 1970.

The episode is a good reminder of how much of pop history is accident. A quiet acoustic track, written by a young man in his early 20s and ignored on release, found a second life through a producer's gamble. Simon had written a song about silence, and it took a drum kit to make the world listen.
